In the spot, a cyclops toy comes to life and becomes enamored with the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max. The toy takes photos, plays games, uses apps, listens to music, captures videos, makes calls, watches TV, and uses the flashlight for shadow puppets. The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max lasts through all of it, remaining at half charge when the cyclops's battery dies and the toy falls asleep. Apple's ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max lasts up to 30 hours in "typical use," which is based on median iPhone usage. The metric includes messages, photo taking, music, social app use, streaming, games, browsing, and navigation. The device lasts for up to 40 hours when streaming video, and up to 45 hours when watching downloaded videos. items.summary: Hong Kong startup Savage Technology has announced its first product, "Orrorin Glasses," promising Vision Pro-style pinch controls and full-color displays for both eyes in a frame weighing just 45 grams. items.body: Hong Kong startup Savage Technology has announced its first product, "Orrorin Glasses," promising Vision Pro-style pinch controls and full-color displays for both eyes in a frame weighing just 45 grams. The company describes the glasses as offering "Vision Pro–level interaction" and being around 25 times lighter than Apple's headset, including its external battery. Savage highlights the bulky hardware currently required for Apple's spatial computing experience, although Orrorin offers substantially fewer capabilities. Savage says small pinches performed at the user's side control the interface without a ring, wristband, or controller. Eye tracking makes the display fade when the wearer looks away, rather than selecting interface elements as it does on Vision Pro. That also distinguishes Orrorin from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, which costs the same $799 but has a screen for only the right eye and requires a Neural Band wristband for gesture control. Standard Ray-Ban Meta glasses have no displays. Orrorin lacks positional tracking and spatial mapping , so it cannot anchor virtual windows in a room like Vision Pro. Orrorin is the first product from Savage Technology, co-founded by Bill Pei and Elena Shi, and remains in engineering validation for now. The company is currently targeting developers with third-party apps and interaction with AI agents such as Claude Code and Codex. Apple is expected to launch its first smart glasses next year , although the initial model reportedly will not have displays, instead offering speakers, microphones, and Siri integration. Orrorin reservations start at $29 toward the $799 price. Savage estimates shipments will begin in March 2027 for Founder Edition buyers and May 2027 for Early Bird buyers. items.body: Apple has rules in place that are supposed to protect iPhone users from unwanted advertising in push notifications and Live Activities, but some apps appear to be flouting these rules, and Apple does not appear to be consistently enforcing them. Apple's App Store guidelines do allow iPhone apps to send push notifications for promotions or direct marketing purposes, but only if users have "explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed" in the app, and so long as the app provides a method "for a user to opt out from receiving such messages." The guideline, in part: Push Notifications should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app's UI, and you provide a method in your app for a user to opt out from receiving such messages. Unfortunately, there are some examples of apps ignoring this guideline. On my iPhone in Canada, there are several apps that send me push notifications containing promotions without offering a way to opt out of these promotion-specific notifications, such as Cineplex, McDonald's, and Wendy's. Canadian food delivery app Skip does offer a setting to turn off promotional notifications, but it has continued to send them to me long after I opted out. TL;DR

• Following multiple previews of the Nothing Ear note, the company has shared a teaser video of the earbuds.

• We’re getting a closer look at the Ear note’s key elements, including the large charging case, the earbuds themselves, and a USB-C port, among other details.

• The Ear note will break cover on December 8, with the company claiming it will offer “best in-ear audio ever.”

Nothing recently shared more details on the Ear note, a pair of earbuds with a charging case that doubles as an AI audio recorder. The company has now shared a video detailing its new hardware ahead of the December 8 launch.

In a video posted to YouTube and social media platforms, Nothing offers a good look at the Ear note’s design from multiple angles, highlighting the charging case’s hardware buttons, a USB-C port, and more.

While the video offers a decent look at the earbuds and the charging case/AI recorder, the description walks through some features and calls it Nothing’s “best in-ear audio ever.”

A Bloomberg report earlier this week revealed a bulk of the Ear note’s features, with CEO Carl Pei noting at the time that this is the company’s first step toward “building a hardware context layer for AI.” Nothing co-founder Akis Evangelidis shared a similar sentiment shortly after the video teaser was published.

Based on what we know so far, the Ear note will record calls through both the earbuds and the charging case, with the latter featuring a couple of handy buttons to start recording instantly. The companion app can turn all recordings into summaries and transcripts, with support for Nothing’s AI voice assistant alongside other AI agents.

Pricing information is currently unavailable, and that’s unlikely to change until the company announces the Ear note on December 8.

Nothing released the Ear 3a earlier this year with audio and call recording support. However, the Ear note takes it a step further with its charging case that serves as a standalone audio recorder.

We’re also eager to learn whether the Ear note’s audio performance holds up against the best earbuds in the segment. The company saying this is its best in-ear audio product is certainly encouraging news.

items.title: Samsung quietly expands Modes and Routines with AI and 7 presets in One UI 9.5
items.summary: You can ask Gemini or Perplexity, but only Perplexity answers automatically.
items.body:

Mobile

Samsung quietly expands Modes and Routines with AI and 7 presets in One UI 9.5

You can ask Gemini or Perplexity, but only Perplexity answers automatically.

•

Nov 25, 2026 — 10:06 AM ET

•

•

Adamya Sharma / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• One UI 9.5 Beta 1 adds an “Ask AI assistant” action to Samsung’s Modes and Routines app that can send prompts to Gemini or Perplexity.

• In our testing, Perplexity automatically sends prompts and reads answers aloud hands-free, whereas Gemini only prefills the prompt and waits for a manual tap because the Google app blocks Samsung’s auto-send request.

• The update also unlocks text summarization, offline translation, image text extraction, and a Repeat loop action. There are also seven new preset routines, including a Morning news briefing that only works hands-free when switched to Perplexity.

Samsung’s Modes and Routines has quietly become one of the most useful parts of One UI for power users. It lets you automate almost anything on your Galaxy phone with simple “if this, then that” rules. With the One UI 9.5 beta, Routines can now hand tasks to an AI assistant as well. Samsung didn’t mention this in the One UI 9.5 beta changelog, but we tried it on our Galaxy S26 Ultra, and which AI assistant you pick makes a big difference.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

Routines can now ask Gemini or Perplexity for you

Modes and Routines v5.2.00.69 in One UI 9.5 Beta 1 adds a new action called “Ask AI assistant.” You pick an assistant, type a prompt into the “Enter command” box, and the routine sends it whenever its trigger fires, whether that’s dismissing your alarm, arriving at work, or tapping a button. The prompt can also include text from earlier actions in the routine, going up to 8,000 characters.

Gemini and Perplexity are the only two options for Ask AI assistant, and they appear only if their apps are installed. Both are built into the Routines app, so you can’t add other AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude. Routines still has a separate “Ask Bixby” action from One UI 9, too.

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

There’s a catch, though: Routines can only launch the assistant. It doesn’t wait for an answer or receive one from the assistant, so you can’t feed the AI’s response back into a later action like a pop-up or a note. The routine finishes as soon as the assistant opens.

Perplexity answers on its own, but Gemini waits for you

With Perplexity, Routines opens the app’s floating assistant with the prompt and tells it to send the prompt right away:

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

In our testing, once the routine was triggered, Perplexity searched the web, answered in its overlay with sources, and read the answer aloud, without us touching the phone.

Gemini is a different story, though. Routines first tries to send the prompt automatically through a Google app service. If that fails, it falls back to sharing the text with the Gemini app, which only prefills the prompt.

On our Galaxy S26 Ultra, the Google app (v17.76.14) rejected Samsung’s request, so Routines used the fallback. Gemini opened full screen with our prompt typed in, and then waited for us to tap Send (which kind of defeats the convenience of a routine).

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Seemingly, the Google app only lets Google’s own apps use this service (for now), so Samsung’s automation has to stop halfway. Google could add Samsung Routines to that allowlist before One UI 9.5’s stable release. Until then, Perplexity is the only assistant that works hands-free in a routine. This is a nice win for Samsung’s growing partnership with Perplexity, even though the limitation likely comes from Google’s side.

The new Morning news briefing preset doesn’t work as advertised with Gemini

This disparity in auto-send behavior in Perplexity vs Gemini matters most for one of the seven new preset routines. “Morning news briefing” runs when you dismiss your alarm, and Samsung describes it like this:

Code

<string name="preset_name_morning_news">Morning news briefing</string>
<string name="preset_description_morning_news">When you dismiss your alarm, a summary of the latest news in society, business, and the stock market is read aloud.</string>
<string name="preset_param_morning_news">Summarize today's top news in 2-3 highlights for society, business, and the stock market.</string>

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

However, the preset’s only action is Ask AI assistant, and it’s set to Gemini by default. There’s no separate read-aloud step in the preset. As a result, with Gemini, you’ll dismiss your alarm and find the news prompt sitting unsent in Gemini. Nothing gets read back to you automatically.

When you switch the assistant to Perplexity, you get the spoken briefing Samsung promises.

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Routines also learns to summarize, translate, and read text from images

The One UI 9.5 beta also adds several more actions:

• “Summarize text” condenses text from earlier in the routine. It runs on Samsung’s servers and needs a Samsung account. It also won’t work if you’ve turned on “Process data only on device” for Galaxy AI, except for the Timeline style.

• “Translate text” runs entirely on your phone using Samsung’s offline language packs.

• “Extract text from image” reads text from a picture, such as your latest screenshot.

• “Repeat” loops actions in a routine.

Summarize and Translate existed in One UI 9’s Routines app, but were hidden and not accessible to users. One UI 9.5 makes them available to everyone.

These actions power some of the new presets. “Screenshot translation,” for example, extracts text from your screenshot, translates it, and shows the result in a pop-up. In One UI 9.5 Beta 1, though, the preset can’t be saved because its “Screen captured” trigger isn’t active yet. When we rebuilt it with a manual trigger, it translated a Settings screenshot into Hindi in a couple of seconds, entirely on the device.

Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Seven new preset routines are ready to use in the One UI 9.5 Beta 1

One UI 9.5 adds seven new preset routines in total, which you’ll find under Discover > New preset routines:

• Pomodoro timer: Get notified at the start of each 25-minute focus session followed by a 5-minute break.

• Monthly media cleanup: Once a month, your duplicate photos and old media files are shown for you to review and delete.

• Screenshot translation: When a screenshot is taken, text from the image is translated and shown in a pop-up.

• Morning news briefing: When you dismiss your alarm, a summary of the latest news in society, business, and the stock market is read aloud.

• Meeting recorder: A meeting is recorded, transcribed, and summarized, then saved as a note with the date and time.

• Plank workout routine: Get a voice guide for three sets of 1-minute planks and rest intervals.

• Monthly storage cleanup: Once a month, your old download files, installation files, and unused apps are shown for you to review and delete.

Samsung hasn’t mentioned any of these Routines changes in its One UI 9.5 beta changelog, but they’re already live in the beta, so you can try them if you’ve installed it. Things could still change before the stable release, especially if Google lets Routines automatically send prompts to Gemini. If you’re on the beta, try the Morning news briefing preset with Perplexity, and let us know in the comments below how it works for you.

Samsung quietly expands Modes and Routines with AI and 7 presets in One UI 9.5
You can ask Gemini or Perplexity, but only Perplexity answers automatically.

blocks.alt: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra Digital AI Assistants Google Perplexity

blocks.text: Adamya Sharma / Android Authority
Add Android Authority on Google:
Preferred Source
Google Discover
TL;DR

items: One UI 9.5 Beta 1 adds an “Ask AI assistant” action to Samsung’s Modes and Routines app that can send prompts to Gemini or Perplexity.

In our testing, Perplexity automatically sends prompts and reads answers aloud hands-free, whereas Gemini only prefills the prompt and waits for a manual tap because the Google app blocks Samsung’s auto-send request.

The update also unlocks text summarization, offline translation, image text extraction, and a Repeat loop action. There are also seven new preset routines, including a Morning news briefing that only works hands-free when switched to Perplexity.

blocks.text: Samsung’s Modes and Routines has quietly become one of the most useful parts of One UI for power users. It lets you automate almost anything on your Galaxy phone with simple “if this, then that” rules. With the One UI 9.5 beta, Routines can now hand tasks to an AI assistant as well. Samsung didn’t mention this in the One UI 9.5 beta changelog, but we tried it on our Galaxy S26 Ultra, and which AI assistant you pick makes a big difference.
APK teardown
This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →
Routines can now ask Gemini or Perplexity for you

Modes and Routines v5.2.00.69 in One UI 9.5 Beta 1 adds a new action called “Ask AI assistant.” You pick an assistant, type a prompt into the “Enter command” box, and the routine sends it whenever its trigger fires, whether that’s dismissing your alarm, arriving at work, or tapping a button. The prompt can also include text from earlier actions in the routine, going up to 8,000 characters.

Gemini and Perplexity are the only two options for Ask AI assistant, and they appear only if their apps are installed. Both are built into the Routines app, so you can’t add other AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude. Routines still has a separate “Ask Bixby” action from One UI 9, too.

blocks.alt: Ask AI assistant action in Samsung Routines showing Gemini and Perplexity

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

There’s a catch, though: Routines can only launch the assistant. It doesn’t wait for an answer or receive one from the assistant, so you can’t feed the AI’s response back into a later action like a pop-up or a note. The routine finishes as soon as the assistant opens.
Perplexity answers on its own, but Gemini waits for you
With Perplexity, Routines opens the app’s floating assistant with the prompt and tells it to send the prompt right away:

blocks.alt: Samsung Routines code sending a prompt to Perplexity with auto-send enabled

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority
In our testing, once the routine was triggered, Perplexity searched the web, answered in its overlay with sources, and read the answer aloud, without us touching the phone.

Gemini is a different story, though. Routines first tries to send the prompt automatically through a Google app service. If that fails, it falls back to sharing the text with the Gemini app, which only prefills the prompt.

On our Galaxy S26 Ultra, the Google app (v17.76.14) rejected Samsung’s request, so Routines used the fallback. Gemini opened full screen with our prompt typed in, and then waited for us to tap Send (which kind of defeats the convenience of a routine).

blocks.alt: Gemini with a prompt from a Samsung routine prefilled but not sent

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Seemingly, the Google app only lets Google’s own apps use this service (for now), so Samsung’s automation has to stop halfway. Google could add Samsung Routines to that allowlist before One UI 9.5’s stable release. Until then, Perplexity is the only assistant that works hands-free in a routine. This is a nice win for Samsung’s growing partnership with Perplexity, even though the limitation likely comes from Google’s side.
The new Morning news briefing preset doesn’t work as advertised with Gemini

This disparity in auto-send behavior in Perplexity vs Gemini matters most for one of the seven new preset routines. “Morning news briefing” runs when you dismiss your alarm, and Samsung describes it like this:
Code

<string name="preset_name_morning_news">Morning news briefing</string>
<string name="preset_description_morning_news">When you dismiss your alarm, a summary of the latest news in society, business, and the stock market is read aloud.</string>
<string name="preset_param_morning_news">Summarize today's top news in 2-3 highlights for society, business, and the stock market.</string>

blocks.alt: Morning news briefing preset set to Ask AI assistant with Gemini

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

However, the preset’s only action is Ask AI assistant, and it’s set to Gemini by default. There’s no separate read-aloud step in the preset. As a result, with Gemini, you’ll dismiss your alarm and find the news prompt sitting unsent in Gemini. Nothing gets read back to you automatically.
When you switch the assistant to Perplexity, you get the spoken briefing Samsung promises.

blocks.alt: Perplexity reading a morning news summary triggered by a Samsung routine

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority
Routines also learns to summarize, translate, and read text from images
The One UI 9.5 beta also adds several more actions:

items: “Summarize text” condenses text from earlier in the routine. It runs on Samsung’s servers and needs a Samsung account. It also won’t work if you’ve turned on “Process data only on device” for Galaxy AI, except for the Timeline style.
“Translate text” runs entirely on your phone using Samsung’s offline language packs.
“Extract text from image” reads text from a picture, such as your latest screenshot.

blocks.text: Summarize and Translate existed in One UI 9’s Routines app, but were hidden and not accessible to users. One UI 9.5 makes them available to everyone.

These actions power some of the new presets. “Screenshot translation,” for example, extracts text from your screenshot, translates it, and shows the result in a pop-up. In One UI 9.5 Beta 1, though, the preset can’t be saved because its “Screen captured” trigger isn’t active yet. When we rebuilt it with a manual trigger, it translated a Settings screenshot into Hindi in a couple of seconds, entirely on the device.

blocks.alt: Samsung Routines pop-up showing a screenshot translated into Hindi

blocks.text: Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority
Seven new preset routines are ready to use in the One UI 9.5 Beta 1
One UI 9.5 adds seven new preset routines in total, which you’ll find under Discover > New preset routines:

items: Pomodoro timer: Get notified at the start of each 25-minute focus session followed by a 5-minute break.
Monthly media cleanup: Once a month, your duplicate photos and old media files are shown for you to review and delete.
Screenshot translation: When a screenshot is taken, text from the image is translated and shown in a pop-up.
Morning news briefing: When you dismiss your alarm, a summary of the latest news in society, business, and the stock market is read aloud.
Meeting recorder: A meeting is recorded, transcribed, and summarized, then saved as a note with the date and time.
Plank workout routine: Get a voice guide for three sets of 1-minute planks and rest intervals.
Monthly storage cleanup: Once a month, your old download files, installation files, and unused apps are shown for you to review and delete.

blocks.text: Samsung hasn’t mentioned any of these Routines changes in its One UI 9.5 beta changelog, but they’re already live in the beta, so you can try them if you’ve installed it. Things could still change before the stable release, especially if Google lets Routines automatically send prompts to Gemini. If you’re on the beta, try the Morning news briefing preset with Perplexity, and let us know in the comments below how it works for you.

items.body:
Apple Has iPads Running macOS Internally, Says Gurman

Wednesday November 25, 2026 4:55 am PST by Tim Hardwick

Apple has iPads running macOS internally and has had them "for some time," according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, although he says no work is currently being done to bring the Mac operating system to iPads.

Speaking on his latest Power On podcast, Gurman said there is "no work being done to consumerize macOS on the iPad." Rather, Apple will continue to bring Mac features and apps like Final Cut to iPadOS piece by piece. Gurman also argued that per-operating-system EU regulation gives Apple an incentive to keep distinct systems for each device. Apple recently dismissed merging iPadOS and macOS.

items.body:
美国纽约州签署法案，限制汽车厂商对预装功能收取订阅费

2026年11月24日，美国纽约州州长凯西·霍楚尔签署一项编号为S.9348A/A.10411A的法案。该法案自2027年2月27日起生效，规定汽车制造商、经销商以及第三方服务提供商不得针对使用预装组件或硬件、且不会产生持续性成本的汽车功能，额外提供订阅服务或在车辆售出后收取费用。
法案将于2027年2月27日生效，违者每个销售点每次违规最高罚款250美元。

在法案签署前，汽车经销商莫霍克雪佛兰（MohawkChevrolet）总裁AndyGuelcher表示，订阅制有助于维持汽车基础售价，消费者可以按照自身需求启用部分功能。
